title: Short-term rental by-law deferred; new artist in residence
subtitle: Committee also backed a Doon Pioneer Park community centre public artwork, with insurance and staffing questions on rentals unresolved.
overview: The committee recommended appointing Tara Cooper as the 2025 Artist in Residence. The residency includes a community-built public artwork for the new outdoor patio at Doon Pioneer Park Community Centre. Residents will take part in workshops that shape the design, and installation is planned for the first half of next year.

The main item was the proposed short-term rental by-law, which would create licence categories, fees and one new staff position. Several rental hosts said the City's indemnification requirement would push their insurance from home to commercial coverage and raise costs sharply. Staff and the City's risk manager said indemnification clauses are standard and are not normally what drives premiums up. The committee went into closed session for legal advice, then voted to defer the matter to the June 23 Council meeting {{vote:m3}}. Staff will bring back more on indemnification, definitions, staffing needs and public feedback.

For residents, no short-term rental licensing rules are in place yet. Council will take up the question again before its summer break. Residents may speak again on June 23 only if they bring new information.

decisions.item: 2025 Artist in Residence and Doon Pioneer Park public art
decisions.detail: The committee recommended appointing Tara Cooper as the 2025 Artist in Residence and approving the proposed artwork at Doon Pioneer Park Community Centre, subject to staff review and an agreement authorized by the Mayor and Clerk.

The committee voted to refer the by-law, its fees and the request for one new full-time position to the June 23 Council meeting so staff can report on indemnification, definitions, staffing needs and public feedback {{vote:m3}}.

debate: Delegates who host short-term rentals said the indemnification requirement would force them into commercial insurance and raise their costs several times over. Some suggested a simple registration system with proof of existing liability insurance instead of licensing.

Staff and the City's risk manager said indemnification and additional-insured clauses are standard across many licence types, and that higher premiums usually reflect added risk rather than the clause itself. The risk manager said they are not a licensed broker and could not say how home insurers classify these policies.

Delegates also questioned how a rental is classed as commercial or as a principal residence, and asked what personal information would be made public. One delegate argued that non-principal-residence rentals should not be treated differently.

Councillors who backed deferral wanted clearer insurance information and said some residents had raised noise, property upkeep and condo concerns. Those who opposed it said the by-law adds cost and bureaucracy and that existing by-law enforcement could handle noise and parties, and one said the program could not be supported by one new staff position.

For the artist in residence, councillors spoke in favour of the community-focused proposal. Staff said combining the residency with the one per cent public art program is a one-off experiment for now.
